title: YOUR MARRIAGE WAS NEVER ONLY ABOUT YOU
paragraphs: YOUR MARRIAGE WAS NEVER ONLY ABOUT YOU
Why the covenant between husband and wife carries a breathtaking picture of Christ, the Church, the cross, forgiveness, and the Gospel that can rewrite even the most wounded love story.
There is a moment in almost every marriage when the photographs stop telling the truth.
The wedding pictures still hang on the wall.
Two people smiling.
Hands intertwined.
Promises spoken.
Family watching.

Maybe somebody cried when the bride walked down the aisle. Maybe the groom could barely get the words out. Maybe both of them believed, with everything inside them, that love would always feel the way it felt that day.
And then came Tuesday.
Bills.
Exhaustion.
Misunderstandings.
Words spoken too sharply.
Words that should have been spoken but never were.
The strange loneliness of lying inches away from someone who suddenly feels miles away.
The argument that supposedly started over dishes but was never really about dishes.
The silence in the car.
The slammed door.
The apology that came too late.
The resentment nobody admitted was growing.
And sometimes, tragically, wounds far deeper than ordinary conflict—betrayal, abandonment, deception, cruelty, or years of pain.
Then somewhere inside the heart comes a terrifying question:
Is this what marriage became?
But there is another question Scripture forces us to ask.
What if marriage was never ultimately designed merely to make two people happy?
What if God placed something inside marriage that reaches beyond romance, compatibility, attraction, children, companionship, or growing old together?
What if marriage was designed to whisper something about Jesus?
That changes everything.
Because when the apostle Paul speaks about marriage in Ephesians 5, he suddenly seems unable to talk about a husband and wife without talking about Christ and His Church.
He writes:
—Ephesians 5:25
The Greek is piercing:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas, kathōs kai ho Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian kai heauton paredōken hyper autēs.
The command ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate means “love.”
But Paul does not leave husbands to invent their own definition of that love.
He gives them a Person.
Christ.
And then he gives them an action.
Christ “gave himself up” for His Church.
The Greek παρέδωκεν — paredōken carries the sense of giving over, handing over, delivering up.
Suddenly biblical marriage becomes far more demanding than flowers, anniversaries, romantic captions, and saying “I love you.”
A husband is pointed toward the crucified Christ.
Not toward domination.
Not toward intimidation.
Not toward selfish entitlement.
Not toward using Scripture to control a woman.
Toward Christ.
The One who gave Himself.
The One who loved sacrificially.
The One whose strength was displayed not through selfish exploitation but through self-giving love.
That means a man cannot use Ephesians 5 to excuse cruelty and still claim he is representing the Christ of Ephesians 5.
Jesus is the standard.

And wives are not presented as spiritually inferior. Scripture teaches that male and female alike bear God's image, and in Christ believers share equally in the inheritance of grace. The biblical vision of marriage cannot honestly be twisted into permission for abuse, coercion, violence, or dehumanization.
Christ does not authorize sin simply because someone has a wedding ring.
That matters.
Especially for the person reading this who has heard the word “submission” weaponized while the command to love like the crucified Christ was conveniently ignored.
But Paul goes deeper.
He reaches backward—all the way to Genesis.

“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”
—Ephesians 5:31, echoing Genesis 2:24
Genesis says:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vehayu levasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two roommates sharing expenses.
Not merely two lovers sharing a bed.
Not merely two names written on a certificate.
A covenantal union with profound bodily, relational, and spiritual significance.
Then Paul says something astonishing.

“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
—Ephesians 5:32
Read that again.
Paul has been speaking about marriage, but suddenly he pulls back the curtain.
Christ and the Church.
The Greek says:
τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν
to mystērion touto mega estin
“This mystery is great.”
Marriage is not the Gospel.
Your spouse is not your savior.
Marriage does not redeem sinners.
Only Jesus does.
But Christian marriage is given the extraordinary vocation of reflecting something beyond itself.
Covenant.
Faithfulness.
Sacrifice.
Union.
Forgiveness.
Sanctifying love.
And a Bridegroom who refuses to abandon His redeemed Bride.
That is why the Gospel gives marriage both its beauty and its discomfort.
Because eventually marriage exposes you.
It reveals how easy unconditional love sounded when it was still theoretical.
It reveals impatience.
Pride.
Selfishness.
The hunger to be right.
The desire to keep score.
The tendency to remember another person's failures while conveniently forgetting your own.
Marriage has a frightening ability to place a mirror in front of the soul.
You thought the biggest problem was that your spouse left the towel on the floor.
Then you discovered the anger underneath your irritation.
You thought the problem was that they did not understand you.
Then God exposed how little effort you sometimes made to understand them.
You wanted grace when you failed.
Justice when they failed.
Mercy for your weakness.
A courtroom for theirs.
And suddenly the Gospel is no longer an abstract doctrine discussed on Sunday.
It is standing in your kitchen at 11:47 at night asking whether you will forgive.
It is sitting beside you after the argument.
It is confronting your pride when you know you should say, “I was wrong.”
It is asking whether you want reconciliation more than you want victory.
And perhaps that is one reason marriage can hurt so deeply.
We are sinners trying to love sinners.
The person standing beside you at the altar did not marry a finished product.
Neither did you.
Two imperfect people entered a covenant, each carrying histories, fears, habits, expectations, family patterns, weaknesses, temptations, and places still needing the transforming grace of Christ.
That does not excuse sin.
Grace never means pretending evil is good.

Forgiveness does not require calling abuse acceptable, eliminating wise boundaries, refusing lawful protection, or preventing appropriate consequences. Reconciliation and restored trust may require repentance, truth, safety, accountability, and time.
But the Gospel does something extraordinary.
It destroys our illusion that only the other person needs grace.
At the foot of the cross, both husband and wife meet as sinners who need a Savior.
And this is where marriage begins reflecting something breathtaking.
Not when two perfect people never disappoint each other.
But when two people repeatedly discover that Jesus is more faithful than either of them.
Think about the scandal of the Gospel.
Humanity rebelled against God.
We sinned against the One who gave us life.
We did not climb our way back to Him through moral achievement.
God came toward sinners.
Jesus Christ entered our broken world, lived without sin, gave Himself on the cross, and rose from the dead.
The innocent One bore what the guilty could never repair themselves.
Peter writes:
—1 Peter 2:24
Paul writes:
—Romans 5:8
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we finally deserved Him.
While we were still sinners.
This does not mean spouses become one another's atoning sacrifices. Christ's sacrifice is unique, sufficient, and unrepeatable.
It means the cross permanently changes the Christian definition of love.
Love is no longer merely:
You make me feel good, therefore I love you.
The cross teaches:
I will seek your true good even when love costs me something.
That is why Christian marriage can become a living signpost pointing toward Jesus.
Every sincere apology whispers the Gospel.
Every act of undeserved kindness whispers the Gospel.
Every decision to put selfishness to death whispers the Gospel.
Every moment when truth defeats secrecy whispers the Gospel.
Every time repentance replaces defensiveness, something beautiful happens.
Every time forgiveness is offered without pretending the wound was insignificant, grace becomes visible.
Every time a husband chooses sacrificial tenderness over selfish power, he points beyond himself.
Every time a wife walks in faithful, Christ-centered love and wisdom, she points beyond herself.
Every time two believers kneel before Jesus and admit, “Lord, we cannot do this without You,” marriage remembers what it was always supposed to remember.
Christ.
Maybe your marriage does not feel like that right now.
Maybe reading this hurts.
Maybe you remember when you prayed together.
Now you barely speak.
Maybe intimacy has become mechanical or disappeared.
Maybe your house is filled with noise but your marriage is filled with silence.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you are doing wonderfully.
You know otherwise.
Maybe your Facebook pictures look happier than your bedroom feels.
Maybe you have become experts at pretending.
And maybe there is something you have not told anyone.
A hidden conversation.
A growing bitterness.
Pornography.
Emotional distance.
A secret account.
A lie.
An attraction you keep feeding.
A refusal to forgive.
A heart already rehearsing life without the person sleeping beside you.
Listen carefully.
Do not confuse concealment with peace.
Darkness grows wherever truth is continually refused.
But this is precisely where the Gospel becomes more than religious language.
Jesus specializes in meeting sinners where the carefully constructed image collapses.
He does not merely decorate broken people.
He resurrects.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He transforms.
He calls sin what it is—and then calls sinners out of it.
That is grace.
Grace is not God whispering, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace is God declaring that sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross, and that His mercy is powerful enough that your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Repentance therefore is not the enemy of marriage.
Sometimes repentance is where resurrection begins.
“I lied.”
“I neglected you.”
“I became cruel.”
“I stopped listening.”
“I have been selfish.”
“I betrayed your trust.”
“I have been hiding.”
“I need help.”
“I sinned against you.”
“Please forgive me.”
Those sentences can feel humiliating.
But pride has buried more intimacy than confession ever did.
And sometimes the holiest moment in a marriage is not a beautiful anniversary dinner.
Sometimes it is a trembling confession at a kitchen table.
Sometimes it is tears.
Sometimes it is counseling.
Sometimes it is accountability.
Sometimes it is finally telling the truth.
Sometimes it is a husband and wife realizing they cannot repair themselves and crying out to Christ together.
Because Jesus does not enter marriage merely to make bad marriages prettier.
He comes to transform people.
And transformed people begin loving differently.
The husband starts asking not merely, “Does she respect me?” but, “Does my life make it easier for her to see the sacrificial character of Christ?”
The wife begins asking not merely, “Does he understand what I need?” but, “Am I responding as someone whose deepest identity and security are rooted in Jesus?”
Both begin asking:
“What needs to die in me so Christ can be seen more clearly?”
Pride?
Lust?
Control?
Resentment?
Selfishness?
Bitterness?
The obsession with winning?
The addiction to being validated?
That is where marriage becomes a discipleship ground.
Not because marriage saves you.
Because Jesus saves you—and then refuses to leave you unchanged.
And there is something else we cannot miss.
The Bible's story of marriage does not end with an earthly husband and wife growing old together.
It ends with a wedding.
Revelation declares:

“Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.”
—Revelation 19:9
The story is moving somewhere.
Toward Christ.
Toward His redeemed people.
Toward the Bridegroom and His Bride.
Toward the day when every temporary earthly sign gives way to the ultimate reality.
That means even the healthiest Christian marriage is not the destination.
Jesus is.
And this matters deeply for single Christians, widows, widowers, divorced people, and those who may never marry.
The Gospel does not make unmarried believers second-class citizens.
Jesus Himself was unmarried.
Marriage is a sign.
Christ is the substance.
No human spouse can fill the place only Jesus can occupy.
So if you are married, do not ask your spouse to become your messiah.
They cannot carry that weight.
Your husband cannot save your soul.
Your wife cannot complete what only Christ can redeem.
Marriage becomes healthier when Jesus returns to the center because two people stop demanding from each other what only God can ultimately provide.
And maybe that is what somebody reading this needed tonight.
You have spent years trying to force another human being to heal a wound only Christ can reach.
Come back to Jesus.
Before you demand transformation from your spouse, bring your own heart into His light.
Before you construct another prosecution against them, ask the Holy Spirit to search you.
Before another night disappears into cold silence, consider whether humility needs to speak.
Before temptation convinces you that secret sin will make you happier, remember what secrecy eventually destroys.
Before you abandon prayer because nothing seems to be happening, remember that God often works in hearts long before we can see the evidence.

And where serious harm, abuse, coercion, or danger exists, seeking safety and trustworthy pastoral, professional, or legal help is not a betrayal of biblical faithfulness. Scripture never requires someone to quietly enable another person's violence or wickedness.
But wherever repentance, truth, safety, and willingness remain possible, never underestimate what Christ can do with surrendered hearts.
Maybe your marriage has a scandal.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe the reputation cracked.
Maybe trust collapsed.
Maybe there are consequences you cannot erase.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
It promises something greater.
Sin does not get the final word over everyone who comes to Christ in repentance and faith.
Jesus does.
Peter had denial in his story.
David had catastrophic sin and consequences in his.
Paul had persecution of Christians in his past.
The Church itself is composed not of people who never needed mercy, but of people whose only hope is mercy.
This is Christianity.
Not spotless people presenting résumés to God.
Sinners coming empty-handed to a crucified and risen Savior.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin.
Not by erasing truth.
He rewrites lives through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, sanctification, and grace.
And that may be the most beautiful thing a Christian marriage can ever communicate.
Not:
“Look how perfect we are.”
But:
“Look how desperately we need Jesus.”
Maybe your children need to see that.
Not parents who never disagree.
Parents who know how to repent.
Not parents who protect their pride.
Parents who protect truth.
Not parents who perform Christianity publicly and punish each other privately.
Parents who actually kneel before Christ.
Imagine what children learn when they hear their father sincerely say, “I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Imagine what they learn when they see their mother choose truth over bitterness.
Imagine what they learn when they discover that Christianity is not pretending Christians never fail.
It is knowing where Christians run when they do.
To Jesus.
That is the Gospel your home desperately needs.
And perhaps this article found you before another argument.
Before another secret.
Before another decision.
Before another night of silence.
Do something with what God is exposing.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness can rightly be extended.
Seek wise help where help is needed.
Open the Bible together.
Put Christ back where neither husband nor wife belongs:
at the center.
And if something inside you broke open while reading this, do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest.
There may be another husband or wife reading those same words tonight who thought they were the only one struggling.
Your honesty may remind somebody that they are not alone in needing Christ.
And please do not let this article die on your screen.
There may be a night when anger is louder than grace and you need to read it again.
Send it privately to the couple you have been praying for.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him.
Because the Gospel was never the announcement that good people finally became good enough.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
He reigns.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something this broken world cannot manufacture:
grace.
So tonight, before you look across the room and ask whether your spouse has become the person you hoped they would become, look toward the cross and ask a more dangerous question:
Am I becoming more like the Christ I promised to follow?
Because your marriage was never only about you.
It was never only about them.
At its highest calling, it points beyond both of you.
Toward a Bridegroom with scarred hands.
Toward a Savior who loved at immeasurable cost.
Toward a covenant secured by His blood.
Toward the Christ who does not merely teach us how to love.
He first loved us.

And when the photographs stop telling the whole story, when romance meets reality, when weakness is exposed, and when two imperfect people finally realize they cannot save themselves or each other, perhaps that is where the deepest picture begins to emerge:
The most unforgettable marriages are not the ones without scars—they are the ones whose scars keep pointing to the Savior who still bears His.
